section_summary: This section documents Japanese control and requisition of merchant ships in 1941, including diverted cargo voyages and the claimed immunity of ships used to repatriate passengers. It also covers port expenses, fuel supplies, frozen funds, and British and American discussions about limiting bunkers for Japanese vessels. Later papers include intelligence reports, vessel lists, and a 1942 inquiry into whether Japanese ships were privately or government operated.

subfiles.title: Marine insurers' inquiry about requisitioned Japanese vessels
subfiles.about: Marine insurers request information by cable about Japanese requisition and diversion of ships.
subfiles.summary: The lawyers say the information is for insurers' business and offer to pay cable costs.

subfiles.title: Reply to marine insurers
subfiles.from: J. E. Saugstad, for the Secretary of State
subfiles.about: The Department says it has asked its Tokyo embassy for information on requisitioned ships.
subfiles.summary: The Department promises a further reply when the embassy responds.

subfiles.title: Australian treatment of Japanese vessels
subfiles.about: The note points to a report on Australian asset freezing and the Kasia Maru.
subfiles.summary: References despatch 167 in the frozen-credits file.

subfiles.title: Request for list of requisitioned Japanese ships
subfiles.about: The Department requests a list of requisitioned or diverted ships and the legal basis for their diversion.
subfiles.summary: Marine insurers seek details about ships carrying U.S. cargoes that did not complete their voyages.

subfiles.title: Tokyo report on Japanese ship controls
subfiles.about: The embassy reports ship diversions and explains Japanese government control of merchant vessel movements.
subfiles.summary: Strict secrecy rules prevent the embassy from verifying complete lists of requisitioned or diverted vessels. Consular offices have identified several reported or presumed cases. The Central Marine Transportation Control Association assigns ships under government authority, while the Ships Protection Law gives the Navy further powers; even requests by these agencies could effectively compel a ship's return.

subfiles.title: Navy copy of Tokyo shipping report
subfiles.about: The Department relays Tokyo's findings about requisitioned and diverted Japanese ships.
subfiles.summary: Summarizes the embassy's inability to obtain full lists and names known vessels.

subfiles.title: Answer to insurers on Japanese ship movements
subfiles.from: Thomas Burke, for the Secretary of State
subfiles.about: The Department gives marine insurers its available ship names and an explanation of Japan's control system.
subfiles.summary: The embassy cannot produce comprehensive lists. Its consuls report vessels requisitioned or diverted, and the Department explains the Central Marine Transportation Control Association's powers and the Navy's navigation authority.

subfiles.title: Japanese requisition orders received
subfiles.about: Tokyo reports receipt of Japanese requisition orders and appointments connected with three U.S.-bound vessels.
subfiles.summary: The Foreign Office supplied orders for the Tatuta, Hikawa, and Taiyo and named officials assigned to vessel operations and passenger or mail business. The second section lists additional names.

subfiles.title: Custody of Japanese requisition documents
subfiles.about: The embassy asks whether to forward copies of Japanese requisition papers.
subfiles.summary: It assumes the copies are for embassy information unless instructed otherwise.

subfiles.title: Copy to naval operations of requisition-document telegram
subfiles.about: A copy relays the embassy's question about forwarding Japanese requisition papers.
subfiles.summary: Duplicates Grew's October 20 message.

subfiles.title: Additional vessel supervisors named
subfiles.about: The Foreign Office supplies orders appointing supervisors for the Hikawa Maru and Taiyo Maru.
subfiles.summary: Kuchiro Uyeno and Tomoyoshi Doi are named to take delivery of and supervise the vessels.

subfiles.title: Iguchi conversation on ship expenses and frozen funds
subfiles.about: The Department reports a conversation about paying expenses for three Japanese ships and transferring blocked funds.
subfiles.summary: Iguchi proposed consular accounts for bunkers and port costs; U.S. officials raised no objection to the payment method, subject to later approval of amounts. They also discussed a clearing account for official expenses and Japanese tankers seeking oil at San Francisco. Treasury concerns centered on funds withheld from the Yokohama Specie Bank's New York branch.

subfiles.title: Insurers' inquiry about American cargo in Japan
subfiles.about: Marine insurers ask whether Japan prevented American-owned transshipment cargo from leaving after U.S. asset freezing.
subfiles.summary: The lawyers seek the date and basis of any Japanese refusal and offer to pay for a Tokyo cable.

subfiles.title: Reply on cargo awaiting transshipment at Kobe
subfiles.from: George Atcheson Jr., for the Secretary of State
subfiles.about: The Department explains the suspension of commercial sailings after reciprocal asset-freezing measures.
subfiles.summary: Japanese vessels had made no commercial U.S. sailings since July 26. Three requisitioned vessels were expected to carry passengers rather than commercial cargo. The broader question of obtaining merchandise from Japan remained unresolved.

subfiles.title: Two more liners leave Japan
subfiles.about: A press report describes Japanese liners sailing to repatriate passengers.
subfiles.summary: Hikawa and Taiyo sail after Tatuta, carrying American passengers.

subfiles.title: Departure dates of three requisitioned ships
subfiles.about: The Japanese Embassy provides departure dates for Tatsuta, Hikawa, and Taiyo Maru.
subfiles.summary: Lists their October departures from Yokohama.

subfiles.title: Request for Tatuta Maru immunity opinion
subfiles.about: An attorney asks whether the Tatuta Maru is immune from U.S. legal process.
subfiles.summary: Werner requests a prompt opinion while the vessel is approaching the United States.

subfiles.title: State Department recognition of Tatuta Maru immunity
subfiles.about: The Department states that the requisitioned Tatuta Maru is entitled to immunity from U.S. courts.
subfiles.summary: It recognizes the vessel's official Japanese government mission and resulting jurisdictional immunity.

subfiles.title: Acknowledgment of immunity opinion
subfiles.about: Werner acknowledges the Department's letter concerning the Tatuta Maru.
subfiles.summary: He thanks the Department for its prompt reply.

subfiles.title: Request for requisition dates
subfiles.about: Marine insurers ask for dates when seven named Japanese vessels were requisitioned.
subfiles.summary: The firm again offers to pay cable expenses.

subfiles.title: Instructions to obtain Japanese requisition papers
subfiles.about: The Department reports its acceptance of Japan's immunity claim and requests all supporting documents.
subfiles.summary: The Japanese Ambassador supplied orders for Tatuta, Hikawa, and Taiyo. Hull informed the Attorney General that he accepted the claim and sought court recognition of immunity. The embassy is instructed to mail its copies of all related papers.

subfiles.title: Japanese proposal for another Tatsuta Maru voyage
subfiles.about: Japan proposes a second requisitioned voyage to Honolulu, Los Angeles, and Balboa.
subfiles.summary: Japan seeks entry, supplies, payment from frozen funds, and transport for Japanese nationals affected by Panama's occupation law. It offers facilities for Americans wishing to depart Japan. The embassy recommends favorable consideration.

subfiles.title: U.S. conditional reply on proposed Tatsuta voyage
subfiles.to: American Embassy, Tokyo; repeated to Chungking
subfiles.about: The Department sets conditions for the Tatsuta Maru's proposed U.S. and Balboa calls.
subfiles.summary: The United States has no objection to the visits and would present formal requisition evidence to courts. It would permit fuel and stores for a return voyage and arrange payment from blocked funds or U.S. passenger fares. It makes no mail commitment and asks Japan to allow Americans enough time to obtain exit permits.

subfiles.title: Amano Maru and suspected clandestine arrivals in Costa Rica
subfiles.about: An intelligence report examines Japanese-controlled fishing vessels and suspected illegal entry into Costa Rica.
subfiles.summary: It describes Amano's fishing company, ownership, payments, and possible meetings with arriving Japanese merchant ships. The report suspects crew exchanges but acknowledges the absence of definite evidence. Costa Rica cancelled the Amano Maru's registration on September 8; the writer recommends investigating its commercial connections.

subfiles.title: War Department view on Balboa call
subfiles.about: The War Department raises no objection to Tatsuta Maru calling at Balboa.
subfiles.summary: It expects cash payment for supplies and reserves judgment on any Panama Canal transit request.

subfiles.title: Request for War Department view
subfiles.about: State requests War Department views on Tatsuta Maru's proposed Balboa call.
subfiles.summary: Forwards Grew's Tokyo telegram for comment.

subfiles.title: Payment arrangements at Balboa
subfiles.about: The Department examines how Japan could pay Tatuta Maru's Balboa charges without a local consulate.
subfiles.summary: Iguchi suggests a Panama legation account or cash carried by a legation employee.

subfiles.title: Tokyo announcement of Tatsuta sailing
subfiles.about: Tokyo press reports that arrangements for Tatsuta Maru's voyage are complete.
subfiles.summary: The Foreign Office spokesman announces the planned U.S. voyage.

subfiles.title: Delayed receipt of urgent Tatsuta instructions
subfiles.about: Grew reports late delivery of Washington's instructions about Tatsuta Maru.
subfiles.summary: He urges direct transmission of important telegrams to Tokyo.

subfiles.title: Reply delivered and Tatsuta itinerary
subfiles.about: The embassy delivers the U.S. reply and reports Tatsuta Maru's proposed schedule.
subfiles.summary: The ship is scheduled for Los Angeles on December 14 and Balboa on December 24.

subfiles.title: Fuel sales to Japanese ships in Chile
subfiles.about: The note points to a telegram on oil sales for Japanese ships' homeward voyages.
subfiles.summary: References Chile telegram 477 in another file.

subfiles.title: Japanese tanker cargoes at San Francisco
subfiles.about: The note points to a memorandum on tanker export licenses and payment from South American funds.
subfiles.summary: References a frozen-credits memorandum concerning Itsukushima Maru and Shoyo Maru.

subfiles.title: British Embassy safe-hand paper
subfiles.about: A British Embassy paper is routed to several State Department offices.
subfiles.summary: Substantive text is illegible in the OCR.

subfiles.title: File transfer notation
subfiles.about: A filing note records transfer of document 894.85/666.
subfiles.summary: Transferred to file 300.1115A.

subfiles.title: Cargo manifest of Japanese vessel
subfiles.about: A report summarizes cargo and two passengers on a Japanese vessel sailing via Peruvian ports and Manzanillo.
subfiles.summary: Lists wool, ores, mercury, nitrate, and two Yokohama-bound passengers.

subfiles.title: Inquiry about Asama Maru shipping charges
subfiles.about: Hoover relays intelligence about paying Asama Maru charges from confiscated German assets.
subfiles.summary: The German Embassy in Bern reportedly sought the Dutch East Indies government's position.

subfiles.title: Reported Japanese unloading near Laguna Chacahua, corrected copy
subfiles.about: An unverified report alleges Japanese ships unloaded boxes near Laguna Chacahua.
subfiles.summary: The source's reliability is unknown; a military attaché was asked to investigate.

subfiles.title: Reported Japanese unloading near Laguna Chacahua
subfiles.about: An earlier copy reports alleged unloading of boxes by Japanese vessels in Oaxaca.
subfiles.summary: The report rests on an unknown source and notes the lagoon's navigable opening.

subfiles.title: Report of Japanese shipping shortage
subfiles.about: A Turkish Foreign Office official says Japan is already short of shipping.
subfiles.summary: The information comes from Turkey's ambassador in Tokyo.

subfiles.title: Japanese ships with private codes
subfiles.about: The FBI forwards a confidential list of Japanese ships and their private codes.
subfiles.summary: The list was reportedly sent from Buenos Aires to Tokyo before U.S. entry into the war. Pages 217–220 contain a heavily degraded tabulation of vessel names and codes; page 221 carries little legible substance.

subfiles.title: British policy on bunkering Japanese vessels
subfiles.about: British officials discuss limiting fuel supplied to Japanese vessels in South America.
subfiles.summary: British facilities generally provide enough fuel for the next port or Japan. Noel Hall favors delaying Japanese ships carrying strategic materials and coordinating tighter limits.

subfiles.title: British policy on bunkering Japanese vessels, duplicate
subfiles.about: A second copy records the discussion of British fuel limits for Japanese ships.
subfiles.summary: Repeats the next-port fuel policy and British interest in delaying vessels carrying strategic materials.

subfiles.title: Assessment of U.S. bunkering policy
subfiles.about: A State Department memorandum identifies gaps in its policy for fueling Japanese ships.
subfiles.summary: It says the policy reaches only some fuel suppliers, lacks a clear British agreement, does not distinguish ships' destinations, and has not been widely circulated.

subfiles.title: Japanese vessels in Latin American ports
subfiles.from: J. J. Reinstein, using Ensign Blake's information
subfiles.about: The memorandum lists Japanese vessels in or bound for South American ports.
subfiles.summary: It records vessel locations, tonnages, routes, and fuel information from the Office of Naval Intelligence.

subfiles.title: Telephone inquiry on Japanese ship bunkers
subfiles.about: Wyndham White asks about progress on bunkering policy for Japanese vessels in Latin America.
subfiles.summary: Reinstein says the Department is considering current ships and possible future arrivals.

subfiles.title: Telephone inquiry on Japanese ship bunkers, duplicate
subfiles.about: A second copy records White's inquiry about Japanese-vessel bunkering policy.
subfiles.summary: Duplicates the September 8 telephone memorandum.

subfiles.title: Japanese vessels in Latin American ports, clearer copy
subfiles.from: J. J. Reinstein, using Ensign Blake's information
subfiles.about: A clearer copy lists Japanese ships, routes, and tonnage in Latin American waters.
subfiles.summary: It includes vessels at Buenos Aires, ships on the South American west coast, and sailings from Japan.

subfiles.title: Inquiry into public or private ownership of Japanese ships
subfiles.about: Counsel seeks evidence of Japanese ship ownership for a California sales-tax proceeding involving Mitsubishi oil sales.
subfiles.summary: The attorney asks whether listed vessels were private carriers or government operated when they entered California ports between 1938 and 1941. He explains Mitsubishi's supervised liquidation under Treasury licenses. Attached lists record vessel entries at San Pedro and San Francisco.

subfiles.title: Lists of Japanese and Axis ships in Far Eastern waters
subfiles.about: The embassy transmits British lists of Japanese merchant vessels and Axis ships in Japanese-controlled waters.
subfiles.summary: The despatch describes the lists' sources and warns that some blockade runners' locations are uncertain. It names three ships known to have run the blockade and notes ongoing British analysis. Copies and microfilm are being shared with U.S. agencies.
